Chapter 13: Essential Trace and Ultratrace
Minerals
Introduction to Trace Minerals
Trace minerals, also known as microminerals, are essential
for human health and are required in small amounts (less
than 100 mg per day). Some elements are categorized as
ultratrace minerals, needed in amounts less than 1 mg per
day. This chapter covers the essential trace minerals (iron,
zinc, copper) and ultratrace minerals (selenium, iodine,
molybdenum, manganese, chromium), along with their food
sources, digestion, absorption, transport, functions,
interactions, excretion, recommended intakes, deficiency,
and potential toxicity.
Iron


Iron is present in the human body at approximately 2-4 g,
found predominantly in hemoglobin (over 65%), with a
stable presence in ferric (Fe3+) and ferrous (Fe2+) forms.
The body absorbs iron from heme (animal sources) and
nonheme (plant sources) foods, with various influences on
absorption including dietary factors, enhancers like vitamin
C, and inhibitors like phytic acid. Recommended intake is 8
mg for adult men and 18 mg for women.
Zinc
Zinc, present in 1.5-3.0 g in the body, plays roles in immune
function, protein metabolism, and wound healing. It is
absorbed mainly in the small intestine through proteins like
ZIP4 and can be influenced by dietary factors, with
absorption ranging from 20-30%. Adult recommendations
are 11 mg for men and 8 mg for women, with increased
needs during pregnancy.
